newsitem.title: USA: United Tech sees 15 pct 1997 EPS growth.
newsitem.headline: United Tech sees 15 pct 1997 EPS growth.

text.p: Industrial conglomerate United Technologies Corp is on track for earnings per share growth of 15 percent to around $7.80 in 1997, company President and Chief Executive George David told reporters on Tuesday.

"What we have said to (analysts) is that we are comfortable with their 15 percent EPS growth forecast... and another year of good-sized, positive cash flow," David said after speaking at an economic conference.
United Technologies' subsidiaries make elevators, air conditioners, automotive components, aircraft engines and helicopters.

Asked whether ongoing aerospace and defense industry consolidation might lead to a marriage between United Tech's Sikorsky Aircraft and rival Bell Helicopter Textron Inc., David said Sikorsky was always interested in growth by acquisition.

"Sikorsky is a very profitable company," he said. "It's after all the biggest helicopter company in revenues in the world. It's got 25 percent share in the total helicopter revenues, so it seems like we ought to be a survivor in this process, and not a seller."
"Everybody in the helicopter business is always talking to each other (about possible tie-ups)," he said.
David said that UTX's Otis Elevator Co. and Carrier Corp. businesses had "terrific" growth prospects in Asia.
"We do more than $5 billion worth of volume in Asia right now, we have 30,000 employees in Asia... and there's a pretty good chance we're the largest single American employer in Asia."

He said Asia's increasing urbanization -- including projections that some 700 million people will move to cities from rural areas in the next 20 years -- would help power the company's growth in the region.
David said United Technologies had no plans to diversify. "We like our present six businesses a whole lot."

Asked about subsidiary Pratt & Whitney's joint venture with General Electric Co, to build an engine for Boeing Co 's proposed longer-range 747, David said the two partners were making "dynamite" progress.
"Revenue service entry is 2001 for Boeing Co, and we will be ready when the airplane is ready," he said.
GE and Pratt will spend $500 million each over four years on the engine project, said David.
